text: The 7th All-Africa Games (Zulu: imiDlalo yesi-7 yase-Afrika; Afrikaans: 7de Afrika-Spele), also known as Johannesburg 1999 (Zulu: eGoli 1999), was a sporting event held from 10 to 19 September 1999 in Greater Johannesburg, South Africa. Fifty-three countries participated in eighteen sports, with netball included as a demonstration sport. South Africa hosted approximately 25,000 visitors, including 6,000 athletes and 3,000 officials from across the continent. The opening ceremony featured dancing, African parables, and Zulu warriors, but due to the size of the props, it was held in an arena with fewer than 15,000 spectators. South Africa, which had lost its bid to Greece for the 2004 Olympic Games, aimed to impress FIFA in hopes of securing the 2006 World Cup, ultimately winning the 2010 edition. The games were a success, with South Africa outperforming Nigeria and Egypt in the medals race. Challenges included 600 children contracting food poisoning after eating boxed lunches during the practice session for the opening ceremony, laborers striking outside venues and displaying placards that read "No Wages, No All Africa Games," the demotion of women's field hockey to a non-medal event after Nigeria withdrew, a melee at the end of an Angola–Egypt basketball game that required police to escort the Egyptian team from the court, and Haile Gebrselassie, the world record holder in the 5,000 and 10,000 meters, opting out for health reasons, removing one of the event's major attractions. Despite these issues, IOC President Juan Antonio Samaranch commended South Africa's organization, stating, "this shows that you can organize big events." Olympic stars Maria de Lurdes Mutola (athletics, 800 m), Penny Heyns (swimming), and Gete Wami (athletics, 10,000 m) excelled in women's events. South African pole vaulter Okkert Brits won his second African Games gold medal, and Assefa Mezgebu of Ethiopia claimed the men's 10,000 m title. Cameroon defeated Zambia 4–3 on penalties to win the football final, becoming the second team to win the tournament twice. Maria de Lurdes Mutola of Mozambique secured her third consecutive 800 meters title. Nigeria won all four relay races—men's and women's 4x100 meters and 4x400 meters. South African men won all four throwing events. New women's events introduced included pole vault, hammer throw, and the 10-kilometre road walk. The tournament's soccer champion was Cameroon, and the coach was Ben Bamfuchile.
